text: Alma S. Woolley (October 3, 1931, New York City – December 17, 2005, Baltimore) was an American nurse, nurse educator, nursing historian, and author. She led several schools of nursing and authored numerous books and articles on nursing education, the history of nursing education, and nurses. Woolley grew up during the Depression in the Bronx, New York City: her father died after being hit by a truck on his way to a public hospital; her maternal grandmother, who worked in a sweatshop, made all her clothes; her widowed mother worked as a stenographer for GM; and at age twelve, Woolley admired the smart gray uniforms with red trimming of the Cadet Nurse Corps during World War II, leading to her selection to attend the elite all-girls Hunter College High School, which she commuted to by public transport one hour each way. At Hunter, she won the all-city Latin Poetry Contest in 1949 and graduated second in her class, then attended Queens College and Cornell University's School of Nursing, earning a bachelor's degree in 1954. She joined the Visiting Nurse Service of New York, married, and worked at hospitals including Mary Immaculate Hospital in Jamaica, Queens, and later at Philadelphia General Hospital and Jefferson Medical College after moving to Philadelphia with her husband, Arthur E. Woolley. She became a nursing instructor at the University of Pennsylvania, enrolled in their graduate program, and earned an M.S. in medical-surgical nursing in 1965, an achievement that led to her early article in The American Journal of Nursing, "My Lamp Is Refueled," explaining how and why she maintained her professional engagement while raising four small children. In 1969, after moving to New Jersey with her husband and children, Woolley became an instructor at Atlantic Community College and was soon offered the task of creating a B.S. degree program in nursing for The Richard Stockton College of New Jersey, which opened in 1971. The original program she designed was for registered nurses, R.N.'s, without a university degree, to complete a Bachelor of Science in nursing. Woolley advocated for the transition of nursing education from non-university-trained R.N.'s to 4-year B.S.N. programs or their equivalents and published several pieces demonstrating the benefits of university-based nursing programs. In 1980, she earned a doctorate in nursing education from the University of Pennsylvania. In 1981, she was appointed Director of the School of Nursing at Illinois Wesleyan University and the Caroline F. Rupert Professor of Nursing; in 1986, she left Wesleyan to become Dean of Georgetown University School of Nursing and Health Studies. In 1989, she received the Distinguished Alumnus Award from the Cornell School of Nursing Alumni Association. She stepped down as dean of Georgetown's School of Nursing in 1992 and returned to teaching and writing, retiring as professor emeritus of nursing in 1996 and becoming a visiting professor at both the University of Maryland School of Nursing in Baltimore, Md, and the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences. She wrote or contributed to biographies of nurses including Maude Francis Essig, who served with American combat troops in World War I, and Virginia Matthews Dunbar, an early advocate of university curricula for nurses. Reflecting her belief that "the history of nursing education is an important lacuna in general histories of nursing" and that "as part of public history in the United States, nursing education can cite many accomplishments in the realm of health care policy," Woolley also published histories of nursing schools, including "Nuns and Guns" and Learning, Faith and Caring. Before her death in 2005, she was working on oral histories of women who, like her, had been recently admitted as members to the once all-male Cosmos Club of Washington, D.C.
